sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Camden County?
sections.html:
Three layers share the work in Camden County. The municipal assessor sets the value of each parcel, the municipal tax collector sends the bill and takes payment, and the Camden County Board of Taxation hears assessment appeals. The board sits at 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood, takes the public Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., and answers at 856-225-5238.

A single bill covers several taxing bodies. In Cherry Hill, the county's most populous town, the township's own 2026 breakdown shows the county levy at 18.86 percent of an average bill, with the school district taking the biggest share. Owners in the other towns see a different mix, so the back of your bill is the place to check your own split.

  • Name or mailing address changes go through the municipal assessor's office, in writing.
  • Questions about how much you owe or when it is due go to your town's tax collector.
  • Questions about a value you think is too high go to the county board, after you talk to your assessor.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Camden County itself?
sections.html:
Camden County covers 221.36 square miles of land along the Delaware River, directly across from Philadelphia, and its ground is flat and low. Its highest surveyed point is about 219 feet above sea level. The county seat is the city of Camden, incorporated in 1828, and the county is split into 36 municipalities, from dense river towns to the wooded suburbs near Voorhees and Cherry Hill.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate puts the population at 535,799, up from 523,500 at the April 2020 base. The median value of an owner-occupied home was $287,100 for 2020 through 2024, owners live in 64.7 percent of households, and median household income was $88,755. The home value sits well below the $524,100 median in Essex County, so price a Camden County house against nearby sales, not against north Jersey numbers.

  • Employers include Campbell's and Subaru of America, both headquartered in the county, plus medical schools run with Rowan University in Camden and Stratford.
  • The PATCO Speedline runs from Philadelphia through Camden to Lindenwold, with stops at Woodcrest, Westmont and Collingswood.
  • Low, flat ground and an aging storm drain system leave parts of the county exposed to flooding, which buyers and inspectors look at closely.

sections.h2: When can you appeal a Camden County assessment?
sections.html:
You can file with the county board from the time assessment notices go out until April 1 at 4:00 p.m., or 45 days after the town finishes mailing its notices, whichever date comes later. The petition has to be received by then. A postmark does not count, and a late petition is dismissed.

Towns that have just finished a revaluation or reassessment get a one-month extension to May 1. The board's website names the towns in that position for the current cycle, and a deadline that lands on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day. Bills for added or omitted assessments, which come from new construction or an error on the tax list, follow their own December 1 rule.

Camden County Board of Taxation filing rules, per the board's own instructions
SituationRule
Regular appealReceived by 4:00 p.m. on April 1, or 45 days after bulk mailing of notices if later
Town revalued or reassessedReceived by 4:00 p.m. on May 1
Added or omitted assessmentReceived by December 1, or 30 days after the collector mails those bills if later
Comparable sales evidenceAt the board, assessor and clerk at least 7 days before the hearing
Further appealTax Court of New Jersey, within 45 days of the board's judgment

sections.h2: How do you file an appeal with the Camden County board?
sections.html:
The board accepts petitions online, by mail and in person, and it holds hearings in a virtual format as well as at its Blackwood location. Online filing runs through a site the board names on its appeals page, which works best in Chrome, Safari or Firefox. The paper form is on the board's forms page.

  • File one petition per parcel, with the filing fee attached: $5 under $150,000 of assessed value, $25 up to $500,000, $100 up to $1,000,000, and $150 above that.
  • Send a copy to the assessor and the clerk of your town.
  • Use up to five comparable sales, with block, lot, sale price and deed date. Comparable assessments do not count as evidence.
  • Pay your quarterly installments while the case is open, at least through the first quarter, unless the board relaxes that rule.

Only the value can be appealed, not the tax bill, and the number the board wants proven is market value as of October 1 of the year before the tax year. If the board lowers your value, the judgment is held in place for that year and the next two unless something such as a town revaluation changes it.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid property tax when you sell a Camden County house?
sections.html:
Unpaid tax follows the house, so it has to be cleared before or at closing. New Jersey towns charge 8 percent interest on the first $1,500 of a delinquency and 18 percent above that, counted back to the due date once the grace period passes. Cherry Hill, for example, gives a 10-day grace period and refuses postmarks.

If a town sells a tax lien on your property, the house cannot be sold until the lien is redeemed. A buyer who holds the lien can start foreclosure in state court if it stays open for two years. Ask the collector in your town for a written payoff figure, with interest to a specific date, before you sign a sale contract.

  • Hand the tax bill to the new owner or the title company at sale.
  • Check sewer and water accounts separately, because many towns bill them apart from the tax.
  • If you are behind on several quarters, get the payoff figure early so the closing agent can plan around it.

sections.h2: Which tax relief programs reach Camden County homeowners?
sections.html:
The state's fiscal year 2027 budget funds three relief programs for owners and renters: Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ. The filing deadline for the 2025 application was November 2, 2026, so that window has closed, and the Division of Taxation's relief page is where the next application window is posted.

Locally, the municipal assessor takes the state-mandated deductions: $250 for qualifying veterans, $250 for seniors and disabled owners who meet the income limit, and a full exemption for owners with a 100 percent permanent and total service-connected disability. Each has residency and ownership tests dated October 1 of the year before the tax year. Ask your town assessor for the current application.

faqs.q: Where do I file a property tax appeal in Camden County?
faqs.a: File with the Camden County Board of Taxation, 509 Lakeland Road, Blackwood, NJ 08012, online, by mail or in person. Phone 856-225-5238 for questions. Serve a copy on your town assessor and clerk.

faqs.q: Is the April 1 appeal deadline ever moved?
faqs.a: Yes, for towns that finished a revaluation or reassessment, the deadline becomes May 1, and any deadline on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day. A petition must be received by 4:00 p.m. on that date.

faqs.q: Does an appeal lower my tax bill right away?
faqs.a: No. You keep paying your installments, at least through the first quarter, while the case is pending. A reduction in value carries into later bills and any overpayment is dealt with after judgment.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Camden County house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the unpaid tax, interest and any lien amount are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Get a written payoff from your town's tax collector before you agree on a closing date.

faqs.q: Who sets Camden County tax rates?
faqs.a: Each town's rate comes from the combined school, municipal, county and any special district levies divided by the town's total assessed value. The county board of taxation sets the rate, and your municipal collector bills it.
